articles.title: Dark homes, dry taps, idle factories: Gurgaon hit by 16-hour power cuts amid strike
articles.summary: GURGAON: Thousands of households went without electricity and water, nearly 1,800 manufacturing units faced disruption, and residents took to the streets
articles.body: GURGAON: Thousands of households went without electricity and water, nearly 1,800 manufacturing units faced disruption, and residents took to the streets as a three-day strike by Haryana's electricity department employees crippled power supply across Gurgaon on Thursday.With breakdown complaints going unattended, inverters running out of charge and industrial units struggling to keep production lines operational, the disruption exposed the city's dependence on an uninterrupted electricity supply for even its most basic needs.The strike, called to protest the Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission's (HERC) decision to grant a parallel electricity distribution licence to private company Eleven Power for Gurgaon and Nuh, began affecting supplies from Wednesday night.By Thursday, power cuts had spread across residential colonies, industrial clusters and rural areas, with residents complaining that repeated calls to electricity officials and helplines had failed to bring relief.In several localities, prolonged outages also hit water supply as electricity-dependent boosting stations and household motors stopped functioning. While some residents managed with water stored in tanks, others said their reserves would last only a few hours. In industrial areas, manufacturers turned to diesel generator sets, but these offered only temporary relief, with prolonged use restricted by overheating, cooling requirements and air pollution control norms.The scale of the disruption was reflected in the complaints received by Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam (DHBVN). An official said the department received more than 3,000 complaints within the first 12 hours of the strike, while DHBVN's helplines received around 5,000 outage complaints on Thursday.Residents, however, alleged that neither the helplines nor the officials responsible for local supply were responding adequately.Gurgaon, which has around 8.5 lakh electricity consumers, saw widespread disruption, particularly in Old Gurgaon. Residents said more than 50,000 households in the area were affected on Thursday, with several localities continuing to face outages even after hours of waiting. The agitation also affected Faridabad and Nuh, where residential areas and industrial units reported power cuts.No electricity, no waterFor thousands of families, the immediate concern was no longer just the absence of electricity but the inability to carry out everyday activities, from cooking and studying to securing drinking water.In Sector 9A, around 6,000 families were affected after power supply snapped around 3.30am on Thursday. The outage also affected the boosting station supplying the area, leaving households without water. More than 16 hours later, supply had still not been restored, according to Suraj Bhola, general secretary of the Sector 9A residents' welfare association (RWA).“I have called the officials nearly 50 times, but nobody is responding. There is no electricity at our homes. Inverters have run out, and now there is no water either because the boosting station is affected. How are people supposed to manage their daily needs?” Bhola said.He alleged that the junior engineer was not answering calls, while the sub-divisional officer had cited the strike. The helpline number provided by the district administration had also failed to secure relief, he said. With no clarity on when electricity would return, residents were unable to plan their day or arrange alternative water supplies. Tankers, he added, were also difficult to find.In Hari Nagar, more than 7,000 families were affected after power supply went off around 10pm on Wednesday and remained disrupted for more than 16 hours, residents said. The accompanying water shortage left families struggling to meet basic needs.“People are suffering in their homes, children are struggling to study, and nobody is listening to us. Junior engineer (JE) and SDO are not answering calls. The office has been locked, and there is nobody available to address the complaints,” said Sumit Gujjar, Hari Nagar RWA president.While acknowledging employees' right to protest, Gujjar questioned the impact of the agitation on ordinary residents.“If employees have an issue with the govt, they should take it up with the govt instead of leaving residents without electricity and water,” he said.The uncertainty over restoration was equally distressing for residents of housing societies, where backup systems could not meet every household's needs.At Zara Aavaas, an affordable housing society, residents said power had been unavailable since 5.30am. The backup system covered essential services such as lifts but did not provide electricity to individual flats.Hemant Sharma, a resident, said the outage had created additional difficulties as pollution levels rose and restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) came into force.“On one hand, pollution levels are increasing and GRAP restrictions are in place, while on the other, the prolonged power outage has forced people to run diesel gensets. Many residents have to work from home, but how are they supposed to work without electricity for so many hours? It is even more difficult for people with medical conditions who may depend on electrical equipment or need a comfortable indoor environment,” he said.Residents of Lotus Homz also struggled as the outage continued through the day.“There has been no power supply since 5am. It has become difficult to manage even basic household chores. Even inverter ran out of battery and I had to cook dinner using the light from my mobile phone. We don’t even know when the electricity will be restored. The management has asked residents to move to the community hall, but while we somehow managed today, we don’t know what will happen tomorrow if the power supply remains disrupted,” said resident Anu Gulati.In Rajendra Park, Bhimgarh Kheri and areas near Gurgaon railway station, residents who had been without electricity since 10am staged a protest near the railway station road bridge on Thursday evening. By around 8pm, with the outage stretching to nearly 10 hours, a large number of men and women had taken to the road and raised slogans against the power department.Police personnel reached the spot to pacify the protesters, but residents refused to disperse until electricity was restored. They said the outage had disrupted household work and water supply.“There is no electricity, and there is no water in our homes. How are we supposed to run the water motor without power?” said Rupa, a resident.Residents in Faridabad's New Industrial Township-2 area also took to the streets demanding restoration of power. Police intervened after receiving information about a road blockade and dispersed the protesters after pacifying them. In Nuh, the disruption affected several areas, including Punhana, Nagina and Firozpur Jhirka.Nearly 1,800 manufacturing units hit; industrialists fear losses worth croresThe power crisis extended beyond homes, threatening production schedules and deliveries across Gurgaon's industrial belt.Nearly 1,800 manufacturing units in the Sector 37 and Kadipur industrial areas faced disruption after power cuts began around 10pm on Wednesday. Industrial units in Basai were also affected, with manufacturers reporting that machinery had stopped and production lines had come to a halt.The affected businesses include textile units, export houses, auto component manufacturers and suppliers of food to corporate and commercial establishments. Industrialists warned that a prolonged disruption could lead to losses running into crores of rupees, while delays in production could affect the availability of finished goods and timely delivery of supplies.Deepak Maini, chairman of the Progressive Federation of Trade and Industry (PFTI), said there had been no power supply in Sector 37 since 10pm on Wednesday.“Power cuts at industrial units have brought machinery and production to a halt, impacting business operations. With operations suspended across hundreds of units, the risk of losses has increased,” Maini said.Manufacturers attempted to switch to diesel generator sets, but said these could not sustain continuous industrial operations. Generators need cooling breaks after running for several hours, interrupting production and making them unsuitable as a long-term replacement for grid electricity.“A generator is meant for backup, not regular power supply. After running for several hours, it heats up and needs to be switched off to cool down,” industrialist Vikrant Gupta said.The situation was further complicated by the enforcement of GRAP from Wednesday. With restrictions on generator sets intended to control air pollution in the National Capital Region, industrialists said they faced a difficult choice between keeping operations running and complying with pollution-control requirements. Non-compliant generator sets could face action under the applicable norms.“How are we supposed to run our operations amid so many disruptions? Power is basic to running an industry,” another industrialist said.Manufacturers said the crisis had also exposed the difficulties in getting faults repaired when the regular electricity workforce was unavailable. Maini said DHBVN officials had expressed their inability to resolve the problems, while private vendors could not be engaged to work on high-tension lines and feeders.He argued that the immediate priority should be uninterrupted electricity, regardless of the provider.“If DHBVN is unable to provide the service, there is nothing wrong with allowing private players. We want an uninterrupted power supply, whoever provides it — the govt or a private player,” Maini said.He added that frequent outages had already become a persistent problem for manufacturers, requiring repeated maintenance interventions and disrupting production schedules.Industrialist PK Gupta said the responsibility for ensuring electricity supply rested with the government.“It is the govt’s responsibility to ensure power supply. We pay taxes to the govt,” he said.Industrialists urged the state government to consider invoking the Essential Services Maintenance Act (ESMA), if legally warranted, and make alternative arrangements to restore electricity. Their concerns highlighted the immediate economic cost of the strike even as the broader dispute centred on whether a private company should be allowed to distribute electricity alongside the state-owned discom.Old Gurgaon worst hit as feeders remain out of serviceThe disruption was more widespread in DHBVN's Circle 1, which covers Old Gurgaon, sectors 9 and 10, and Kadipur, than in Circle 2, which includes parts of South City, Sohna and sectors along Golf Course Road.In Circle 1, 12 of the 530 11kV feeders were out of service on Thursday. In Circle 2, 14 of the 750 feeders were shut down.Power supply remained disrupted in nearly 50 localities, including Palam Vihar, New Palam Vihar, Sai Kunj, Chandan Vihar, Ashok Vihar, sectors 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 7 Extension, Hari Nagar, Gandhi Nagar, Rajendra Park, Vishnu Garden, Surat Nagar, Dhanwapur, Sushant Lok 2 and 3, Manesar, Sohna and Taoru.Sector 9A remained among the worst-affected areas, with residents reporting that power had not returned even after several hours. In Sushant Lok 2, around 500 families in B block were without electricity from about 6am. Supply was restored in Sushant Lok around 2.30pm, but Sector 9A was still without power at the time of filing this report.The situation also deteriorated around Sohna and Nimauth power houses. Four feeders were out of service by 8am on Thursday, and the number rose to 12 by 3pm, affecting around 30 villages. Two urban feeders were also disrupted, affecting City-4, Gehlot Bihar and the MVN and Aekam residential societies.Officials said five of the 15 feeders serving rural areas and seven of the 39 urban feeders had been shut down by 3pm.The relatively better situation in parts of Circle 2 was attributed to an arrangement under which line maintenance in selected localities had been outsourced to a private company. Its workers continued attending to faults and breakdowns despite the strike.The arrangement covers areas such as Badshapur, Tikli, Bhondsi, Rithoj, parts of South City and sectors 14, 17, 18 and 23. However, it does not extend across the entire city. Substations and power houses continue to depend on DHBVN employees, limiting the extent to which outsourced maintenance can compensate for the absence of the regular workforce.DHBVN deployed around 100 workers hired through a contractor to repair faults, but the arrangement brought little relief, with workers reportedly struggling to identify the faults.Chief engineer PK Chauhan said the overwhelming participation of employees had made it difficult to handle complaints.“About 98% of DHBVN’s officers and employees are on strike. Even executive engineers and superintending engineers have joined it. The absence of staff is making it difficult to address electricity complaints. Senior officials have been informed about the situation,” he said.In Circle 1, 816 of 826 employees joined the strike, while 540 of 557 employees in Circle 2 stayed away from work. Outsourced staff and workers recruited through Haryana Kaushal Rozgar Nigam also joined the agitation. Superintending engineers Shyambir Saini and Manoj Yadav supported the protest.Subhash Kumar, SDO of Sohna DHBVN, said updates on outages were being shared with senior officials every hour.Helplines fail to provide relief as officials struggle to respondAs complaints mounted, the district administration and electricity department faced criticism from residents who said they had no reliable way to find out when supply would be restored.On Wednesday evening, deputy commissioner Uttam Singh issued a press release listing contact numbers for consumers affected by outages. Residents said, however, that complaints made through toll-free numbers 1912 and 180010804334, as well as WhatsApp numbers 8813999708 and 9540954768, did not result in timely relief.The problem was compounded by the absence of employees at complaint centres, substations and offices at the sub-divisional, divisional and circle levels. The striking employees' joint front said many of these facilities had been largely deserted, while faults affecting 33kV and 11kV feeders remained unattended.The state government said arrangements were being made to maintain supply during the strike, with deputy commissioner Uttam Singh directing officials to prioritise essential services, including hospitals, water supply systems and the metro.But residents said the lack of clear information about restoration was making the disruption harder to manage. In areas where electricity had been unavailable for much of the day, exhausted inverter batteries and depleted water storage left families with few alternatives.Why are electricity employees on strike?The immediate trigger for the strike was HERC's October 19 order granting Eleven Power Private Limited a parallel electricity distribution licence for Gurgaon and Nuh for 25 years under Section 14 of the Electricity Act, 2003.The licence allows the company to distribute electricity in the two revenue districts alongside the existing state-owned distribution companies. The Haryana Bijli Karamchari and Engineers Joint Sangharsh Morcha called a three-day strike against the decision, arguing that the entry of a private distributor threatened the existing public distribution system.Around 40,000 electricity department employees across Haryana joined the strike, according to the unions, which said the agitation was not about salaries or allowances but about protecting public electricity infrastructure, employees' jobs and consumers' interests.Devender Singh Hooda, a senior leader of the joint front, said the movement was aimed at preventing the privatisation of electricity distribution and safeguarding farmers and ordinary consumers.The unions argued that a parallel distribution licence could weaken the revenue base of public utilities in an agriculture-dominated state. They warned that this could affect the ability of public discoms to provide affordable and reliable electricity, particularly to farmers and economically weaker sections in rural and urban areas.The unions also questioned the transparency of the regulatory process. They sought details of Eleven Power's experience, technical capabilities, capital investment, financial strength and eligibility, as well as public disclosure of the criteria used to assess its application. They demanded an impartial inquiry into the roles of the regulator and the company.Amarjeet Jakhar and Mukesh Bhayana said the agitation would continue until the decision was withdrawn. Jakhar said employees would decide whether to extend the strike beyond October 24 if their demands were not accepted.The movement also received support from several workers' and farmers' organisations. Most constituent organisations of the Samyukt Kisan Morcha, along with Sarv Karamchari Sangh Haryana and trade unions, including CITU, AITUC and INTUC, extended support and organised demonstrations at various locations.Subhash Lamba, vice-president of the Electricity Employees Federation of India (EEFI), and Shailendra Dubey, chairman of the All India Power Engineers Federation (AIPEF), also opposed the parallel licence.Lamba alleged that the Haryana government was attempting to undermine the agitation by bringing technical employees and supervisors from neighbouring states, including Punjab and Himachal Pradesh.“If the chief minister and the energy minister oppose privatisation and stand with electricity employees, why is a parallel distribution licence being granted to a private company in the first place?” he asked.He said the government needed to demonstrate its opposition through concrete action rather than assurances.Govt says strike unnecessary, promises legal battle against licenceThe Haryana government has opposed the licensing decision and said it would challenge HERC's order before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), seeking an immediate stay on its implementation.Chief minister Nayab Singh Saini said on Wednesday that the government would represent the employees' case before the tribunal. He also assured unions that lawyers trusted by the employees could be engaged to pursue the challenge.Saini held a review meeting with administrative secretaries and district officials through video conferencing to assess preparations for the three-day strike. He appealed to the unions to call off the agitation, saying the government's doors for dialogue remained open.Energy minister Anil Vij, meanwhile, termed the strike unnecessary, arguing that the licensing decision had been taken by the independent regulator rather than the state government.Vij said the government had opposed the move before HERC and would now challenge it before APTEL. He also said he was against privatisation because substantial public money had been invested in the existing electricity infrastructure and employees' jobs were at stake.“I am against privatisation because substantial public money has been invested in the infrastructure and employees’ jobs are at stake,” he said.Vij urged employees to return to work and participate in the legal challenge instead of continuing the strike. He offered to involve union representatives in preparing the government's case, including by allowing them to advise its lawyer, appoint their own counsel or recommend another lawyer.The government has maintained that it did not invite applications for privatising electricity distribution. However, Vij said the central law allows any eligible individual or company to apply for a distribution licence, and the decision to grant one rests with the regulator.The distinction has become central to the dispute: while the state government says it is opposed to the licence and intends to challenge it, the employees want the decision withdrawn and a clear policy ruling out parallel distribution licences anywhere in Haryana.Power engineers seek cabinet decision to rule out parallel licencesThe dispute escalated on Thursday as electricity engineers and employee representatives called on the state government to go beyond its proposed legal challenge and take a policy decision against parallel distribution licences.AIPEF chairman Shailendra Dubey, along with Haryana Power Engineers Association leaders Puneet Kundu and Ravinder Singh Ghanghas, urged chief minister Nayab Singh Saini to convene a cabinet meeting and announce a policy ruling out such licences anywhere in the state.Dubey said the government should use its statutory powers under the Electricity Act, 2003, to revoke the licence.The employee leaders questioned HERC's decision and alleged that it appeared to promote privatisation despite the state's stated opposition. They demanded transparency on the private company's qualifications and an impartial inquiry into the circumstances in which the licence was granted.The unions said their concerns extended beyond the immediate impact on jobs. They argued that allowing parallel distribution could undermine the financial position of state-owned utilities and eventually affect electricity affordability and reliability for ordinary consumers.The government, however, has maintained that it must challenge the regulator's decision through the appropriate legal process. Vij urged employees to end the strike and join that effort, while Saini assured them that the state would pursue the matter before APTEL.The impasse has left residents and businesses bearing the immediate cost of a dispute over the future structure of electricity distribution.For households, the consequences have been exhausted inverters, dry taps, disrupted routines and uncertainty over when power would return. For manufacturers, they have included idle machinery, production delays and concerns over pollution norms governing backup generators. For the electricity department, the strike has sharply reduced the workforce available to respond to faults across a network serving around 8.5 lakh consumers in Gurgaon alone.With the unions threatening to decide on an extension beyond October 24 if their demands are not accepted, the prospect of further disruption remains a concern. The government is pursuing a legal challenge to the licence, but until the dispute is resolved and normal operations resume, consumers remain caught between the regulator's decision, the employees' opposition and the state's efforts to restore services.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Gurgaon | Silver Rate in Gurgaon | Bank Holidays in Gurgaon | Public Holidays in Gurgaon | Gurgaon AQI | Weather in Gurgaon | Petrol Price in Gurgaon | Diesel Price in Gurgaon | CNG Price in Gurgaon | LPG Price in GurgaonStay updated with the latest Gurgaon news. articles.title: CJP’s Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka, Ajinkya Shinde to face SEM court hearing today after skipping Delhi Police questioning
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde are expected to appear before a Special Executive
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) activists Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde are expected to appear before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court on Friday, even as the Delhi Police Crime Branch continues its investigation into the October 13 Jantar Mantar protest case.The three activists, who were summoned for questioning on Thursday but did not appear, have been asked to join the probe between 10 am and 4 pm, ahead of the court hearing scheduled for 3 pm.CJP activists miss Crime Branch questioningThe Crime Branch had called the three activists to its Rajouri Garden office at noon on Thursday. However, Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and Ajinkya Shinde did not appear before the investigating agency and sought additional time to join the probe.Police are expected to issue fresh notices to the activists. No fresh notice had been issued for Friday, but they have been asked to appear for questioning anytime between 10 am and 4 pm.If the activists decide to join the investigation on Friday, they are expected to appear before the Crime Branch before the SEM court hearing at 3 pm. Their appearance before the investigating agency, however, will depend on their decision.SEM court orders release of CJP leaders from judicial custodyThe latest developments follow an order by the SEM court directing the release of Das and Ranka from judicial custody after accepting their personal and surety bonds and recording written undertakings from them to maintain peace and abide by the law.SEM Ritu Raj directed both leaders to furnish personal and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each, which will remain in force until the conclusion of the enquiry.The court also instructed them to attend every hearing and comply with the conditions laid down in their bonds and undertakings.In their written undertakings, Das and Ranka pledged not to breach peace or disturb public tranquillity. They also agreed not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar until the site is denotified in accordance with the law.Any future demonstrations, they stated, would be conducted within the constitutional framework."Further judicial custody does not appear to be necessary at this stage, particularly after written undertakings before this Court," the SEM court observed while ordering their release.Why were CJP activists detained?Das and Ranka were detained in connection with a protest held at Jantar Mantar on October 13. The site had been denotified as a designated protest venue.According to the police, the activists entered the area through private premises and allegedly violated conditions relating to the maintenance of peace.The case concerns the circumstances surrounding the protest and the alleged breach of the applicable restrictions.The SEM court has clarified that the enquiry into the matter will continue in accordance with the law, despite the release of the two activists from judicial custody.(With ANI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: In 2009, Yosemite treated an 8.65-acre Himalayan blackberry infestation with herbicide; a year later, 0.34 acres of the treated area remained
articles.summary: Discover how Yosemite National Park dramatically reduced the area of invasive Himalayan blackberries by 96% in one year using herbicides and various management techniques. Learn about the ecological impacts of invasive species and the park's ongoing efforts to protect native vegetation.
articles.body: Invasive plants can be hard to control in protected natural areas, especially when they form dense thickets that crowd out native vegetation. Yosemite National Park in California has spent years tackling this problem, using different methods to limit the spread of aggressive non-native plants. One treatment in Yosemite Valley produced a striking result within a year: according to the National Park Service’s Treatment of Invasive Plants page, a Himalayan blackberry infestation fell from 8.65 acres to just 0.34 acres.Herbicide treatment reduced blackberry cover from 8.65 to 0.34 acresThe National Park Service’s Treatment of Invasive Plants page reports that only 0.34 acres remained the following year, a reduction of 96% in a single year and cites the project as an example of how targeted herbicide application can work. Before 2009, Yosemite used only manual and mechanical methods. For fifteen years, park managers and hundreds of volunteers tried to control aggressive invasive plants such as Himalayan blackberry and yellow star-thistle. Even when staff and volunteers controlled some areas, the plants spread faster than they could keep up, so park managers turned to herbicide treatment. The same page says the inefficient use of resources and the need for repeat treatments led managers to adopt herbicides as one of many tools.Dense thickets threaten native vegetationHimalayan blackberry is an introduced shrub that forms thorny thickets. These thickets compete with native plants, can alter the structure and function of the plant community and may block access to sites. Invasive species are a management priority in Yosemite National Park because changes in native vegetation can affect the wildlife that depends on it. Blackberries attract animals, including bears, so their spread near developed areas increases contact between bears and people. The National Park Service discusses these ecological concerns in its overview of invasive plants in Yosemite.Yosemite combines herbicides with other control methodsYosemite National Park uses a combination of manual, mechanical and chemical control, along with monitoring and restoration. Managers choose among these methods based on effectiveness, worker safety and conditions at each site. The National Park Service page says manual removal can be appropriate where herbicide is unsuitable, such as near rare plants, but the soil disturbance it causes can create conditions for other non-native plants to take hold.The National Park Service’s 2024 Invasive Plant Management Program Work Plan names glyphosate applied from backpack sprayers as the main treatment method for Himalayan and cut-leaf blackberry in Yosemite. Crews may instead use the cut-and-dab method, in which plants are cut and herbicide is applied to the stump, near special status plants, important cultural sites, or water.Monitoring remains essential after treatmentThe 96% reduction in the treated area illustrates the effectiveness of targeted applications of herbicides, but this cannot be considered eradication of Himalayan blackberry within Yosemite Valley. This reduction applies only to one patch over one year and results may differ elsewhere. Seeds and regrowth could reestablish plants in treated patches and other invasive plants may move in, so monitoring remains essential. The work plan says crews monitor previously treated sites and retreat as needed. The case shows that managing invasive plants takes more than one step.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2019, a tornado damaged a Texas couple’s home; State Farm paid nearly $293,000, but after a five-day trial, a jury and a 2025 appeals court rejected their claim that more was owed
articles.summary: In a dramatic court case, a Texas couple's claim against State Farm for additional tornado damage reimbursement was rejected by a jury, who upheld the insurer's payout of nearly $293,000. Learn about the legal contest that unfolded over damage assessments, jury decisions, and the appeals process.
articles.body: A tornado can leave a family with two problems at once. Besides the damaged house itself, there is the repair estimate, which arrives later and is rarely in line with what the insurer is willing to pay. The gap between the two figures becomes the point of contention, because insurance covers insured losses rather than guaranteeing a home restored to the owner’s specifications. Few such disputes reach a jury; most end in settlement.Gary and Martha Smith, a couple from Texas, took theirs all the way. The Smiths held a homeowners policy with State Farm Lloyds, and in 2019 a tornado hit their property. State Farm paid them $292,901.67 for covered losses and additional living expenses, but the Smiths felt they deserved considerably more. After a five-day trial, a jury sided with the insurer, and on December 2, 2025, the Fifth Circuit, a US federal appeals court, affirmed the verdict in an unpublished opinion.From inspection to lawsuitAfter the tornado, the insurer sent an inspector to assess the damage. The Smiths were not happy with the assessment and claimed that the company had acted in bad faith, a term that often refers to an insurer arbitrarily withholding money it owes. They wanted $2.5 million before any lawsuit was filed. They sued in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, alleging breach of contract and violations of Texas insurance law. By closing argument, the sum they were asking for had grown to somewhere between $25 million and $250 million. The Smiths said that award should send a message to the insurer. The jury then weighed five days of evidence before reaching its verdict.What the jury heardThe trial lasted for five days and included eight witnesses, 36 factual stipulations, or facts the two parties agreed to in advance, and 384 exhibits. Experts were called in from both sides, but they disagreed fiercely on the extent of the damage. The insurer’s engineer, Joe Shahid, testified that the house could be restored to its pre-tornado condition with minimal modifications. Another expert for the insurer, Gary Boyd, who specialises in construction methods and repair costs, said the Smiths’ estimates were inflated and indicated a full remodel rather than necessary repairs.The Smiths’ own experts disagreed, but a jury is entitled to believe the evidence of one party. The jury found that the insurer had not breached its policy, had not engaged in any unfair or deceptive behaviour and had not failed to pay the whole claim. The appeals court added that the insurer had prepared its own estimate of the damage, shared it with the couple and even offered to resolve any differences in repair costs. The couple’s appeal focused on a procedural misstep by the insurer rather than on the size of the claim.Why the appeal failedThe stumbling block was photographs. Shahid had taken 993 photos of the property and relied on them in part for his report, but the insurer did not turn them over until the eve of trial. That was a breach of the court’s scheduling order and restrictions on disclosure of expert material. The Smiths requested the judge to strike Shahid in its entirety. Instead, the court limited his evidence to the images that had been shared on time, excluded the late ones, struck any mention of them and kept them out of the jury chamber.The appeals court approved their selections. Shahid had been deposed by the Smiths before and they knew his views; therefore, there was nothing surprising about his testimony, it said. The pictures also mostly used images they had already received. The couple had multiple opportunities to ask for a mistrial and at one point rejected the judge’s offer to declare one. The court held that since they had accepted the judge’s directions at the time, they could not dispute the verdict on the same grounds later on.Appeals courts are reluctant to overturn jury verdicts. The Fifth Circuit emphasised the role of the jury, not the judge, in weighing evidence and deciding which witnesses to believe. The verdict is sufficient as long as there is competent evidence in the record to support it. The trial court had also refused to grant a new trial, judging the jury's findings to be sound.But homeowners who believe an offer is too low do have options before a case hits the courtroom. The Texas Department of Insurance proposes submitting documentation, like a contractor’s estimate, to explain the dispute to the insurer, using the policy’s appraisal procedure if available, or filing a complaint with the department. If those measures fail, mediation and litigation remain options.The case of the Smiths is an example of the power of a jury’s judgment when the evidence is presented. The ruling was not published and, as such, is not binding on other courts, but it shows how far a bad faith claim can travel and how a payment of nearly $293,000 can still become the centrepiece of a five-day trial.You use AI every day. articles.title: China’s 'eyes in the sky' multiply, India’s surveillance fleet faces a numbers game
articles.summary: New satellite imagery shows four of China's KJ-3000 Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft at the Xi'an Aircraft Company factory at
articles.body: New satellite imagery shows four of China's KJ-3000 Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) aircraft at the Xi'an Aircraft Company factory at Xi'an-Yanliang, raising the possibility that the type is moving into serial production. The imagery, captured on October 5 and provided by Vantor, shows three KJ-3000s near the factory and a fourth at the nearby China Flight Test Establishment, US based think tank Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies assesses that four aircraft point to serial production.The KJ-3000, also called the KJ-20, is based on the four-engine Y-20B transport with Chinese-made engines. It has a large circular radome above the rear fuselage and an aerial refuelling probe above the cockpit. The first poor-quality photographs appeared in December 2024, and clearer images followed in May 2025. It is meant to address limits in China's existing large AEW&C fleet, since only four KJ-2000 aircraft, built on the Russian Il-76MD, have been completed. The Pentagon's 2025 report on China's military noted the KJ-3000's initial flight.The Chinese armed forces currently operate over around 70 AEW&C aircraft split between the air force and the navy. The most numerous of these is the smaller KJ-500 aircraft. The KJ-500 is based on the Y-9 transport aircraft, which is based on the Soviet An-12.India's own airborne early warning fleet is far smaller. The Israeli Phalcon system on Russian-built Il-76 aircraft came first, under a 2004 agreement with Israel and Russia for three systems. The first aircraft entered service in 2009, with the other two following over the next two years. Its rotating radome gives 360-degree coverage, but three aircraft cannot provide continuous cover across the northern and western airspace.The indigenous Netra Mk I was developed by DRDO's Centre for Airborne Systems on the Brazilian Embraer EMB-145. Its indigenous AESA radar in a dorsal radome gives about 240-degree coverage. The first aircraft flew with its surveillance equipment in 2011, and the IAF received its first Netra in 2017, a second in 2019 and a third in 2023. On June 25, 2026, DRDO handed over the Final Operational Clearance certificate, after the integration of additional electronic-support measures and radar-warning receivers. These aircraft were used during the Balakot airstrikes and Operation Sindoor. As of October 2026, the IAF has three Phalcon and three Netra Mk I aircraft. The air force has an estimated requirement of at least 18 such platforms.The next step is the Netra Mk II, built around six Airbus A321 aircraft acquired from Air India. In July 2026, DRDO's Centre for Airborne Systems (CABS) signed a contract with AI Engineering Services Limited to prepare the aircraft for conversion to military configuration, and a separate contract named Adani Defence Systems and Technologies as development-cum-production partner for the mission systems. Airbus Defence and Space is to deliver the modified aircraft, after which the Indian team will integrate and test the equipment. Separately, in January 2026 the IAF issued a request for information for six more AEW&C aircraft, with at least 10 hours' endurance or air refuelling, high-altitude operation and 360-degree radar coverage.
